source.title: Revisiting dynamic batch scheduling for grokking: the role of batch size, sample budget, and regularization

record.tranche_reason: The study finds that the apparent large-batch advantage depends on whether progress is measured in update steps or a matched sample budget, and that effects vary with weight decay, model size, and task. It refines the scope of batch-size claims in grokking experiments.
record.gate_note: The study measures grokking on algorithmic tasks, not natural-label test error after random-label memorization. It reports batch-size and hyperparameter comparisons relevant to V5. Architecture comparisons, optimizer comparisons, dropout, sharpness measures, and memorized-example removal are not tested. The reported model-size sweep does not test widening past an interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The matched-example experiments test V5 in a new setting: algorithmic classification with transformers. Equal processed-example budgets hold training exposure approximately constant, and larger fixed batches yield worse held-out accuracy. Fixed-update experiments do not test the fixed-epoch claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: large batches improve update-step efficiency but are not necessarily sample-efficient; results depend on task, regularization, capacity, and budget. The authors recommend reporting both update-based and sample-normalized metrics.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a transformer on algorithmic grokking tasks and compares dynamic and fixed batch schedules under update-step and matched-example budgets; it does not test the natural-label generalization settings in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed outcomes vary with measurement budget (update steps versus processed examples), task, weight decay, model dimension, and maximum batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: Large batches improve update-step efficiency when allowed greater total example exposure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In algorithmic grokking experiments, fixed large batches can generalize sooner in update steps while requiring more processed examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight decay changes grokking onset and final accuracy at a fixed batch size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking in these transformers requires sufficient weight decay, and stronger decay can accelerate threshold attainment while reducing final accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Smaller maximum batches yield higher final accuracy under a fixed-update exponential schedule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing the maximum batch size does not monotonically improve final grokking accuracy under fixed update budgets.

record.problems: The study is limited to algorithmic tasks and 7,500 update steps; several results have high variability across seeds. The matched sample budget is only 240,000 examples, and the authors note larger budgets may change the trade-off. Learning rate, optimizer choice, and dataset fraction were held fixed.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted other per-task step-based and matched-budget strategy entries, and further weight-decay/model-dimension entries from Tables 1–3, to keep the extraction focused on the clearest batch-size contrasts and stated conditions relevant to V5. No cited prior-work results were entered as rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting contrasted with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold with training to convergence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.

Image-classification and language benchmarks; longer matched training budgets; interventions in learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization that demonstrably close a batch-size penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Matched processed-example budgets approximate equal epoch exposure on the same training split, making these experiments relevant to V5 in a new task setting. The study does not challenge V5 by finding large-batch advantages at fixed update counts. Other per-task and hyperparameter results are explicitly declared omitted in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweep beyond zero training error and the resulting test-error curve.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance.

Image-classification and language benchmarks; fixed epoch budgets; broader changes such as learning-rate scaling with warmup, normalization, and regularization. The study instead uses algorithmic tasks and compares fixed update-step and matched-example budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training-test gap.
Removing highly memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: Transformer model (fixed batch size 512)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed batch size 512 on modular division under the step-based protocol.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy; mean update steps to that threshold
rows.baseline: Fixed batch size 32: 89.7% mean validation accuracy; 4/10 runs grokked
rows.value: 99.6% mean validation accuracy; 10/10 runs grokked; 3,245 ± 122 update steps
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 10 seeds, as reported.
rows.note: The paper characterizes this as update-step efficiency; batch 512 processes more examples per update.
rows.check: Equal update counts give batch 512 sixteen times the example exposure of batch 32; this comparison cannot establish V5's fixed-exposure effect.

rows.subject: Transformer model (fixed batch size 512)
rows.stage_stated: trained to a matched budget of 240,000 examples
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed batch size 512 under the matched-sample-budget protocol.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy
rows.baseline: Fixed batch size 32 under the same sample budget: 89.7% mean validation accuracy; 4/10 runs grokked
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 10 seeds; table reports 1.6 ± 0.0.
rows.note: The text explicitly contrasts this with fixed-32 performance at the same example budget.
rows.check: The extracted state is reversed: 1.6% versus 89.7% validation accuracy at equal example exposure is the large-batch penalty V5 predicts.

rows.subject: Transformer model (exponential batch schedule)
rows.stage_stated: trained to a matched budget of 240,000 examples
rows.operation_detail: Trained with an exponential increase in batch size under the matched-sample-budget protocol.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy
rows.baseline: Fixed batch size 512 under the same sample budget: 34.1% validation accuracy; 0/10 runs grokked
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 10 seeds, as reported.
rows.note: The paper identifies exponential scheduling as particularly strong on modular addition under the sample budget.
rows.check: Supports the benefit of adapting the batch recipe at equal example exposure: exponential scheduling reaches 98.8% versus fixed-512's 34.1%. It does not isolate a learning-rate or normalization intervention.

rows.subject: Transformer model (fixed batch size 512)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed batch size 512 on modular addition under the step-based protocol.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy; mean update steps to that threshold
rows.baseline: Dynamic exponential schedule: 99.9% mean accuracy and 10/10 runs grokked
rows.value: 99.9% mean validation accuracy; 10/10 runs grokked; 2,135 ± 95 update steps
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 10 seeds, as reported.
rows.note: The article reports fixed-512 as the fastest grokking baseline on this task by update steps.
rows.check: Equal update counts do not hold example exposure fixed. The baseline is another batch schedule rather than a matched-exposure small-batch control.

rows.subject: Transformer model (fixed batch size 512)
rows.stage_stated: trained to a matched budget of 240,000 examples
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed batch size 512 under the matched-sample-budget protocol.
rows.measure: Whether any run reached 99% validation accuracy
rows.value: Never reaches 99% validation accuracy on any task
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the four tasks; per-task values are reported separately in Table 2.
rows.check: Failure to cross 99% alone does not establish worse held-out performance than smaller batches. Add per-task comparison baselines; all strategies fail this threshold on permutations.

rows.subject: Transformer model (fixed batch size 512)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed batch size 512 on modular division while varying weight decay.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy
rows.baseline: Fixed-512 with weight decay 0.5: 99.2 ± 0.8% accuracy; 5/5 runs grokked
rows.note: The text says none of the tested strategies grokked at weight decay 0.
rows.check: This varies weight decay at a fixed batch size, so it cannot establish a batch-size penalty or its recovery. The 1.6% fixed-512 result at zero weight decay is stated in Section 5.2 but is absent from Table 3.

rows.subject: Transformer model (fixed batch size 512)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed batch size 512 on modular division while varying weight decay.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy; update steps to threshold
rows.baseline: Fixed-512 with weight decay 0.5: 99.2 ± 0.8% accuracy; 3,160 ± 150 steps; 5/5 runs grokked
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 5 seeds, as reported.
rows.note: Stronger weight decay accelerated threshold attainment but lowered final accuracy.
rows.check: This compares weight-decay settings at one batch size without measuring whether regularization changes the large-versus-small-batch penalty. All runs crossing 99% is compatible with lower final accuracy because the threshold records first attainment.

rows.subject: Transformer model (exponential batch schedule)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with an exponential batch schedule while varying its maximum batch size.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy
rows.baseline: Maximum batch size 512: 84.3 ± 15.3% accuracy; 5/5 runs grokked
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 5 seeds, as reported.
rows.note: Both settings grokked in all runs; the smaller maximum batch had higher final accuracy.
rows.check: Changing maximum batch size under equal update counts also changes total example exposure; this does not test V5's fixed-exposure comparison.

rows.subject: Transformer model (exponential batch schedule)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with an exponential batch schedule while varying its maximum batch size.
rows.measure: Final validation accuracy; runs reaching 99% validation accuracy
rows.baseline: Maximum batch size 512: 84.3 ± 15.3% accuracy; 5/5 runs grokked
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard error across 5 seeds, as reported.
rows.note: Both settings grokked in all runs; the smaller maximum batch had higher final accuracy.
rows.check: Changing maximum batch size under equal update counts also changes total example exposure; this does not test V5's fixed-exposure comparison.

relationships.condition: Modular division, AdamW with weight decay 0.5, matched budget of 240,000 examples
relationships.reason: R2 shows the large-batch penalty: fixed-512 reaches 1.6% validation accuracy versus 89.7% for fixed-32.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest the larger fixed batch achieved much lower validation accuracy under the matched example budget. These results have not been verified.

relationships.condition: Modular addition, matched budget of 240,000 examples, exponential batch scheduling versus fixed-512
relationships.reason: R3 shows that adapting the batch recipe improves validation accuracy from 34.1% to 98.8%, consistent with recipe-dependent large-batch performance.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest exponential batch scheduling improved validation accuracy over the larger fixed batch. These results have not been verified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Step-based protocol on tested algorithmic tasks
reader_labels.reason: Fixed batch 512 matched or outperformed dynamic schedules by update steps; on modular division it reached 99.6% accuracy with 10/10 runs grokked (R1, R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Matched budget of 240,000 examples on tested algorithmic tasks
reader_labels.reason: The fixed-512 advantage did not persist under equal example exposure: it never grokked across tasks, while exponential scheduling reached 98.8% and 9/10 runs on modular addition (R2, R3, R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Weight decay and maximum batch size varied on modular division
reader_labels.reason: At weight decay 0 fixed-512 did not grok; at 1.0 it grokked faster but had lower final accuracy, and smaller maximum batches produced higher final accuracy than 512 (R6–R9).
